claim: Optogenetically stimulated cholinergic fibers in rat neocortex release acetylcholine that enhances excitability by reducing Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (ERG) K+ current.
source: In this study we optogenetically stimulated cholinergic fibers in rat neocortex and find that ACh enhances excitability by reducing Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (ERG) K+ current.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation experiments combined with pharmacological blockade and voltage-clamp recordings showing ACh-mediated reduction of ERG currents.

claim: ERG mediates the late phase of spike-frequency adaptation in pyramidal cells.
source: We find ERG mediates the late phase of spike-frequency adaptation in pyramidal cells and is recruited later than both SK and M currents.
evidence: Demonstrated through pharmacological blockade experiments showing delayed bifurcation times (~575-600 ms) with ERG antagonists compared to SK and M current blockers.

claim: ERG is recruited later than both SK and M currents during spike-frequency adaptation.
source: We find ERG mediates the late phase of spike-frequency adaptation in pyramidal cells and is recruited later than both SK and M currents.
evidence: Supported by cumulative spike count analysis showing SK modulation at ~75 ms, M current at ~225 ms, and ERG at ~575 ms bifurcation times.

claim: Attenuation of ERG during coincident depolarization and ACh release leads to reduced late phase spike-frequency adaptation.
source: Attenuation of ERG during coincident depolarization and ACh release leads to reduced late phase spike-frequency adaptation and persistent firing.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that ACh release during depolarizing steps reduces adaptation with similar kinetics to ERG blockade.

claim: Attenuation of ERG during coincident depolarization and ACh release leads to persistent firing.
source: Attenuation of ERG during coincident depolarization and ACh release leads to reduced late phase spike-frequency adaptation and persistent firing.
evidence: Shown by current-clamp recordings demonstrating persistent firing following step stimuli paired with ChR2-mediated ACh release, which was abolished by ERG antagonists.

claim: Attenuating ERG enhanced signal-to-noise ratios in neuronal ensembles.
source: In neuronal ensembles, attenuating ERG enhanced signal-to-noise ratios and reduced signal correlation, suggesting that these two hallmarks of cholinergic function in vivo may result from modulation of intrinsic properties.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of virtual ensembles showing increased SNR from 18.6 to 24.0 with ChR2 stimulation, primarily through signal enhancement.

claim: Attenuating ERG reduced signal correlation in neuronal ensembles.
source: In neuronal ensembles, attenuating ERG enhanced signal-to-noise ratios and reduced signal correlation, suggesting that these two hallmarks of cholinergic function in vivo may result from modulation of intrinsic properties.
evidence: Shown by pairwise correlation analysis demonstrating 22% reduction in signal correlation (from 0.27 to 0.21) with ChR2 stimulation.

claim: Enhanced signal-to-noise ratios and reduced signal correlation observed with ERG attenuation are hallmarks of cholinergic function in vivo.
source: In neuronal ensembles, attenuating ERG enhanced signal-to-noise ratios and reduced signal correlation, suggesting that these two hallmarks of cholinergic function in vivo may result from modulation of intrinsic properties.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous in vivo studies showing similar effects during cholinergic stimulation and attention.

claim: Acetylcholine increases the excitability of neurons under in vitro conditions.
source: Abundant work (Sidiropoulou et al., 2009, Zhang et al., 2013, Dembrow and Johnston, 2014) has demonstrated that many neuromodulators, such as acetylcholine (ACh), increase the excitability of a wide variety of neurons under both in vitro (Krnjević et al., 1971, Egorov et al., 2002, Egorov et al., 2006, Rahman and Berger, 2011, Knauer et al., 2013) and in vivo conditions (Metherate et al., 1992, Metherate and Ashe, 1993, Goard and Dan, 2009, Zhou et al., 2011, Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies demonstrating ACh-mediated increases in neuronal excitability.

claim: Acetylcholine increases the excitability of neurons under in vivo conditions.
source: Abundant work (Sidiropoulou et al., 2009, Zhang et al., 2013, Dembrow and Johnston, 2014) has demonstrated that many neuromodulators, such as acetylcholine (ACh), increase the excitability of a wide variety of neurons under both in vitro (Krnjević et al., 1971, Egorov et al., 2002, Egorov et al., 2006, Rahman and Berger, 2011, Knauer et al., 2013) and in vivo conditions (Metherate et al., 1992, Metherate and Ashe, 1993, Goard and Dan, 2009, Zhou et al., 2011, Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous in vivo studies.

claim: Tasks that promote ACh release demonstrate network desynchronization.
source: Yet, studies of circuit activity during tasks that promote ACh release demonstrate more complex changes than expected from a uniform increase in neuronal excitability, including network desynchronization (Metherate et al., 1992, Kalmbach et al., 2012, Pinto et al., 2013, increasing signal-to-noise ratios (SNR, Zinke et al., 2006, Sato et al., 1987, Minces et al., 2017), and reducing correlation of activity levels between neurons (Goard and Dan, 2009, Minces et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing network desynchronization during ACh release.

claim: Tasks that promote ACh release increase signal-to-noise ratios.
source: Yet, studies of circuit activity during tasks that promote ACh release demonstrate more complex changes than expected from a uniform increase in neuronal excitability, including network desynchronization (Metherate et al., 1992, Kalmbach et al., 2012, Pinto et al., 2013, increasing signal-to-noise ratios (SNR, Zinke et al., 2006, Sato et al., 1987, Minces et al., 2017), and reducing correlation of activity levels between neurons (Goard and Dan, 2009, Minces et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating SNR increases with ACh release.

claim: Tasks that promote ACh release reduce correlation of activity levels between neurons.
source: Yet, studies of circuit activity during tasks that promote ACh release demonstrate more complex changes than expected from a uniform increase in neuronal excitability, including network desynchronization (Metherate et al., 1992, Kalmbach et al., 2012, Pinto et al., 2013, increasing signal-to-noise ratios (SNR, Zinke et al., 2006, Sato et al., 1987, Minces et al., 2017), and reducing correlation of activity levels between neurons (Goard and Dan, 2009, Minces et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing reduced correlation during ACh release.

claim: Cholinergic modulation can improve visual discrimination.
source: Together, these effects enable cholinergic modulation to improve visual discrimination (Pinto et al., 2013), enhance sensory coding (Goard and Dan, 2009) and influence attention (Steinmetz et al., 2000, Briggs et al., 2013) and working memory (Goard and Dan, 2009, Ballinger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pinto et al., 2013.

claim: Cholinergic modulation can enhance sensory coding.
source: Together, these effects enable cholinergic modulation to improve visual discrimination (Pinto et al., 2013), enhance sensory coding (Goard and Dan, 2009) and influence attention (Steinmetz et al., 2000, Briggs et al., 2013) and working memory (Goard and Dan, 2009, Ballinger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goard and Dan, 2009.

claim: Cholinergic modulation can influence attention.
source: Together, these effects enable cholinergic modulation to improve visual discrimination (Pinto et al., 2013), enhance sensory coding (Goard and Dan, 2009) and influence attention (Steinmetz et al., 2000, Briggs et al., 2013) and working memory (Goard and Dan, 2009, Ballinger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steinmetz et al., 2000 and Briggs et al., 2013.

claim: Cholinergic modulation can influence working memory.
source: Together, these effects enable cholinergic modulation to improve visual discrimination (Pinto et al., 2013), enhance sensory coding (Goard and Dan, 2009) and influence attention (Steinmetz et al., 2000, Briggs et al., 2013) and working memory (Goard and Dan, 2009, Ballinger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goard and Dan, 2009 and Ballinger et al., 2016.

claim: Previous work has identified a large set of outward and inward currents that could explain the increase in excitability with cholinergic stimulation.
source: Previous work has identified large set of outward and inward currents that could explain the increase in excitability traditionally found with cholinergic stimulation (McCormick and Prince, 1985, Haj-Dahmane and Andrade, 1996, Buchanan et al., 2010, Cui and Strowbridge, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies identifying multiple currents modulated by cholinergic stimulation.

claim: Prolonged application of exogenous agonists can trigger different intracellular signaling cascades than endogenous ligand released synaptically.
source: First, studies employing prolonged application of exogenous agonists can trigger different intracellular signaling cascades than the endogenous ligand does when released synaptically (Davis et al., 2010, Wacker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis et al., 2010 and Wacker et al., 2017.

claim: The range of potential mechanisms defined by bath application of carbachol and related agonists likely includes many non-physiological targets.
source: This limitation suggests that the range of potential mechanisms defined by studies of bath application of carbachol (CCh) and related agonists likely includes many non-physiological targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previous claim about differential signaling cascades with exogenous versus endogenous ligands.

claim: Stimulation-evoked discharges in neocortical pyramidal cells typically have strong spike frequency adaptation.
source: Stimulation-evoked discharges in neocortical pyramidal cells typically have strong spike frequency adaptation (SFA) and, to our knowledge, no group has assayed the effects of endogenous ACh on SFA.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about neocortical pyramidal cell physiology.

claim: No group has assayed the effects of endogenous ACh on spike frequency adaptation in neocortical pyramidal cells.
source: Stimulation-evoked discharges in neocortical pyramidal cells typically have strong spike frequency adaptation (SFA) and, to our knowledge, no group has assayed the effects of endogenous ACh on SFA.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of publication.

claim: Modulation of spike frequency adaptation alone is sufficient to account for increased excitability at the single cell level and many network changes.
source: Previous modeling results, however, suggest that modulation of SFA alone is sufficient to account for both the increased excitability observed at the single cell level as well as many of the network changes (increased SNR, decreased signal correlation, Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014a modeling study.

claim: Acetylcholine influences synaptic function that could contribute to SNR enhancement and reduced network correlation.
source: Acetylcholine also influences synaptic function that could contribute to SNR enhancement and reduced network correlation (Min et al., 2018, Litwin-Kumar et al., 2011, Picciotto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on synaptic modulation by ACh.

claim: Synaptic changes by ACh must occur within the context of altered intrinsic physiology, including adaptation dynamics.
source: However, these synaptic changes must occur within the context of altered intrinsic physiology, including adaptation dynamics, necessitating an integrative approach that includes determining the primary biophysical targets of cholinergic modulation (Marder et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the need to consider both synaptic and intrinsic mechanisms together.

claim: SK, M, and ERG are three primary K+ currents that govern spike frequency adaptation in neocortical pyramidal cells, activated in that order.
source: In the present study, we determined the sequence of activation of three primary K+ currents that appear to govern SFA in neocortical pyramidal cells (SK, M, and ERG in their order of activation).
evidence: Demonstrated through pharmacological blockade experiments showing sequential bifurcation times.

claim: Endogenous ACh released by optogenetic stimulation modulates neuronal discharges by selectively attenuating ERG.
source: Endogenous ACh released by optogenetic stimulation modulates neuronal discharges by selectively attenuating one of these currents (ERG).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing ERG antagonists occlude ACh effects while SK and M current blockers do not.

claim: Acetylcholine acting through mAChRs enhanced intrinsic excitability by selectively reducing the late phase of SFA normally mediated by ERG.
source: Acetylcholine acting through mAChRs enhanced intrinsic excitability by selectively reducing the late phase of SFA normally mediated by ERG.
evidence: Shown by atropine blockade of ACh effects and similarity of ACh and ERG blocker effects on late-phase SFA.

claim: The ACh-triggered changes in excitability and SFA were occluded by three different ERG channel antagonists.
source: The ACh-triggered changes in excitability and SFA were occluded by three different ERG channel antagonists.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with terfenadine, E-4031, and ErgToxin.

claim: Reducing ERG-like linearly increasing K+ currents enhanced network SNR in computational models.
source: Examining consequences of ERG modulation by ACh in virtual ensembles, we find an enhancement in SNR and reduction in signal correlation among neurons similar to that observed in vivo following cholinergic stimulation.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling experiments.

claim: Changes in population neuronal activity associated with attention and working memory could reflect changes of intrinsic biophysical properties modulated by cholinergic input.
source: These results suggest that changes in population neuronal activity associated with common behavioral phenomenon such as attention (Steinmetz et al., 2000, Briggs et al., 2013) and working memory (Goard and Dan, 2009, Ballinger et al., 2016) could reflect changes of intrinsic biophysical properties of individual cells that are modulated by cholinergic input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing that intrinsic property modulation can produce network effects similar to those observed in vivo.

claim: ERG mutations are associated with schizophrenia.
source: Given the established role of ERG mutations in schizophrenia (Huffaker et al., 2009) along with the sensitivity of ERG to many common neuroleptic drugs (Shepard et al., 2007), this biophysical SFA modulation may help explain the association between cholinergic dysfunction and schizophrenia (Sarter and Bruno, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huffaker et al., 2009.

claim: ERG is sensitive to many common neuroleptic drugs.
source: Given the established role of ERG mutations in schizophrenia (Huffaker et al., 2009) along with the sensitivity of ERG to many common neuroleptic drugs (Shepard et al., 2007), this biophysical SFA modulation may help explain the association between cholinergic dysfunction and schizophrenia (Sarter and Bruno, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shepard et al., 2007.

claim: There is an association between cholinergic dysfunction and schizophrenia.
source: Given the established role of ERG mutations in schizophrenia (Huffaker et al., 2009) along with the sensitivity of ERG to many common neuroleptic drugs (Shepard et al., 2007), this biophysical SFA modulation may help explain the association between cholinergic dysfunction and schizophrenia (Sarter and Bruno, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarter and Bruno, 1998.

claim: ChR2 stimulation of nucleus basalis axons increased the number of action potentials evoked by depolarizing steps in 84% of L5 pyramidal cells.
source: Combining light-stimulated ACh release (20 Hz trains of 2 ms light pulses) with depolarizing steps consistently increased the number of APs evoked by depolarizing stimuli (observed in 84% of experiments).
evidence: Reported as a direct experimental observation from the study.

claim: ChR2-mediated ACh release resulted in 39% more spikes within 2 s depolarizing steps in 5 cells.
source: As demonstrated in the example recording shown Figure 1A–B, the increase in excitability evoked by endogenous ACh resulted in 39% more spikes within the same 2 s depolarizing step (N = 5 cells; quantified in Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1A-D with quantification from 5 experiments.

claim: ChR2 stimulation of NB axons alone (without temporally overlapping intracellular depolarization) did not modulate the membrane potential over a 2 s window.
source: ChR2 stimulation of NB axons alone (without a temporally overlapping intracellular depolarization) did not modulate the membrane potential over the 2 s window we typically used to assay excitability changes or directly trigger discharges (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1E-F and supplementary figure.

claim: No statistically significant changes in neuronal input resistance were found following light pulse trains presented alone.
source: We found no statistically significant changes in neuronal input resistance following light pulse trains presented alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown in supplementary figure 1B.

claim: Light pulse trains had no effect on depolarizing step responses in four neocortical pyramidal cells from age-matched control animals without AAV-ChR2 injections.
source: In addition, we found no effect of light pulse trains on depolarizing step responses in four neocortical pyramidal cells from age-matched control animals without AAV-ChR2 injections (no significant difference in membrane potential modulation or the number of spikes evoked by depolarizing steps, both p>0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Demonstrated in control experiments without ChR2 expression.

claim: The increase in neuronal excitability with paired ACh release was repeatable across multiple trials.
source: The increase in neuronal excitability we find with paired ACh release was repeatable across multiple trials with no modulation of excitability observed in interleaved control trials without ChR2 stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure 1C.

claim: The excitability modulation by ACh was unaffected by bath application of antagonists for ionotropic glutamate and GABA receptors.
source: The excitability increase also appeared to be a direct action on the recorded neuron rather than from an enhancement of synaptic excitation since the excitability modulation was unaffected by bath application of antagonists for ionotropic glutamate and GABA receptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; N = 3).
evidence: Demonstrated in 3 experiments shown in supplementary figure 1D.

claim: Release of endogenous ACh selectively advanced the timing of APs triggered after ~500 ms from the step onset.
source: Unexpectedly, the increase in neuronal excitability elicited by ACh was not uniform during the response to the depolarizing step. Instead, release of endogenous ACh selectively advanced the timing of APs triggered after ~ 500 ms from the step onset (Figure 1B and G).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: Only ChR2 stimulation that temporally overlapped with current steps increased the number of spikes evoked.
source: The only timing paradigm that increased the number of spikes evoked occurred when current steps temporally overlapped the light stimuli. ChR2 stimulation before the current had no direct effect on the step response and ChR2 stimulation following the step failed to trigger discharges (Figure 1I).
evidence: Demonstrated in 7 experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Only ACh release that was coincident with the current step modulated the afterpotential, converting the afterhyperpolarization into an afterdepolarization.
source: Only ACh release that was coincident with the current step modulated the afterpotential, converting the afterhyperpolarization into an afterdepolarization (Figure 1J–K).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1J-K.

claim: The afterdepolarization following coincident step and ChR2 stimulation was abolished by atropine.
source: Like the enhancement in excitability, the afterdepolarization following coincident step and ChR2 stimulation was abolished by atropine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure 1E.

claim: The magnitude of light-evoked enhancement of neuronal excitability was unaffected when steps were paired with light pulse trains whose frequency varied from 5 to 40 Hz.
source: The magnitude of light-evoked enhancement of neuronal excitability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B) and afterpotential modulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) was unaffected when steps were paired with light pulse trains whose frequency varied from 5 to 40 Hz.
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure 2A-C.

claim: The degree of excitability enhancement varied between weak and strong depolarizing steps with more additional spikes produced with strong steps.
source: However, the degree of excitability enhancement did vary between weak and strong depolarizing steps with more additional spikes produced when ChR2 stimulation was combined with strong steps than with weak steps (Figure 2B, inset).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2B inset.

claim: Pairing light stimulation with 100 ms step stimuli did not increase the number of APs evoked in 5 cells.
source: We confirmed that prediction by testing responses to 100 ms step stimuli and found no increase in the number of APs evoked with stimulation (6.0 ± 0.0 with step only vs 6.0 ± 0.0 with step + light; N = 5).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in 5 cells.

claim: Pairing light stimulation with longer duration steps (750-2000 ms) increased the number of APs in the same 5 cells.
source: In the same 5 cells, pairing light stimulation with longer duration steps (750–2000 ms) increased the number of APs directly demonstrating the specificity of ChR2 modulation to long-duration responses in these experiments (20.2 ± 0.7 with step only vs. 24.8 ± 0.4 with step + light; N = 5; p<0.001; paired t-test).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the same 5 cells tested with 100 ms steps.

claim: Modulating the delay between ChR2 stimulation and the depolarizing step by 3 s had no significant effect on the enhancement in neuronal excitability.
source: We found that modulating the delay between ChR2 stimulation and the depolarizing step by 3 s had no significant effect on either the enhancement in neuronal excitability or SFA dynamics.
evidence: Demonstrated in experiments varying ChR2-to-step latency shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Stimulating ChR2 mid-way through a 4 s step depolarization increased the number of APs evoked.
source: As shown in the example trace in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, stimulating ChR2 mid-way through the step depolarization still increased the number of APs evoked (quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B ).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure 1A-B.

claim: The latency from initial ChR2 light stimulus to functional effect (increased firing rate) is approximately 520 ms based on ISI analysis.
source: First, we determined the first inter-spike interval (ISI) that was reduced following ChR2 stimulation (compared with the mean ISI immediately before light stimulation). This ISI-based analysis method likely provides a lower bound on the signaling latency (~520 ms; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Calculated from experiments shown in supplementary figure 1C.

claim: ChR2-stimulated ACh release can modulate channel function and increase neuronal excitability within 500-700 ms.
source: This latency, 675 ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) is only modestly longer than the lower bound estimate and suggest that ChR2-stimulated ACh release can modulate channel function and increase neuronal excitability within 500–700 ms.
evidence: Inferred from the ISI and Δ1AP time measurements.

claim: Under all three timing conditions, ChR2 reduced SFA and promoted near tonic firing based on ISI ratio measurements.
source: Finally, we confirmed using conventional early/late ISI ratio measurements that under all three timing conditions ChR2 reduced SFA and promoted near tonic firing (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2G.

claim: ERG is expressed in L5 neocortical pyramidal cells.
source: Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (ERG) K+ channel is likely a potential candidate as we (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) and others (Saganich et al., 2001, Papa et al., 2003) previously demonstrated that ERG is expressed in L5 neocortical pyramidal cells and functions to dampen neuronal excitability.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: ERG functions to dampen neuronal excitability in L5 neocortical pyramidal cells.
source: Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (ERG) K+ channel is likely a potential candidate as we (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) and others (Saganich et al., 2001, Papa et al., 2003) previously demonstrated that ERG is expressed in L5 neocortical pyramidal cells and functions to dampen neuronal excitability.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of mAChRs with bath CCh can inhibit ERG.
source: We also recently demonstrated (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) that activation of mAChRs with bath CCh can inhibit ERG.
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Whole-cell ERG-mediated currents take hundreds of ms to develop when tested using voltage-clamp steps from the resting potential of L5 neurons.
source: When tested using voltage-clamp steps from the resting potential of L5 neurons, whole-cell ERG-mediated currents take hundreds of ms to develop (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018, Niculescu et al., 2013), mimicking the slow SFA kinetics we find.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blocking ERG with terfenadine increased baseline excitability during control conditions and occluded the light-stimulated enhancement of spike discharge.
source: As shown in Figure 3A–B, we find that blocking ERG with terfenadine (Terf) increased baseline excitability during control conditions (without ACh release) and did indeed occlude the light-stimulated enhancement of the spike discharge (no statistically significant increase in number of APs when light and the step were presented together).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Blockade of ERG reduced the ADP response evident following the step response when ACh was present.
source: Blockade of ERG also reduced the ADP response evident following the step response when ACh was present (orange arrowhead in example trace in Figure 3A; ADP quantified in Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A and quantified in Figure 3C.

claim: E-4031 abolished the ACh-mediated enhancement in step responses (N=3).
source: Two other chemically different ERG antagonists, E-4031 and ErgToxin, also abolished the ACh-mediated enhancement in step responses (N = 3 for each antagonist; light stimulation evoked 5–6 additional spikes in the step response in each experiment before blocking ERG and on average < 1 additional spike after ERG blockade).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in 3 cells.

claim: ErgToxin abolished the ACh-mediated enhancement in step responses (N=3).
source: Two other chemically different ERG antagonists, E-4031 and ErgToxin, also abolished the ACh-mediated enhancement in step responses (N = 3 for each antagonist; light stimulation evoked 5–6 additional spikes in the step response in each experiment before blocking ERG and on average < 1 additional spike after ERG blockade).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in 3 cells.

claim: M current antagonist XE991 failed to occlude the light-stimulated enhancement of step discharges (N=3).
source: By contrast, antagonists of both the M current and SK channels failed to occlude the light-stimulated enhancement of step discharges (M current:~5 extra spikes evoked by step + light both with and without XE991, N = 3; SK: 4–7 extra spikes evoked both with and without NS8593, N = 3).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in 3 cells.

claim: SK channel antagonist NS8593 failed to occlude the light-stimulated enhancement of step discharges (N=3).
source: By contrast, antagonists of both the M current and SK channels failed to occlude the light-stimulated enhancement of step discharges (M current:~5 extra spikes evoked by step + light both with and without XE991, N = 3; SK: 4–7 extra spikes evoked both with and without NS8593, N = 3).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in 3 cells.

claim: ChR2-stimulated ACh release selectively reduced the late phase of outward currents evoked by depolarizing steps without affecting the initial current response.
source: Over ten similar experiments, ChR2-driven ACh release selectively reduced the late phase of the outward currents evoked by depolarizing steps (1802 ± 312 pA in control to 1522 ± 293 pA with ChR2 stimulation; p=3.23e-05, T = 7.630) without affecting the initial current response assayed over the first 100 ms (1354 ±381 pA in control vs 1326 ± 380 pA; p>0.05; T = 1.772; both paired t-tests; Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated in 10 voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ChR2-sensitive outward current began ~0.5 s after the depolarizing step onset.
source: On average, the ChR2-sensitive outward current began ~ 0.5 s after the depolarizing step onset (summary plot in Figure 4C) and developed with kinetics well fit by single exponential functions (mean tau = 1.2 s; Figure 4D), consistent with previous work on ERG kinetics (Sturm et al., 2005, Wang et al., 1996, Wang et al., 1997a).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4C from 10 experiments.

claim: The ChR2-sensitive outward current developed with kinetics well fit by single exponential functions with mean tau = 1.2 s.
source: On average, the ChR2-sensitive outward current began ~ 0.5 s after the depolarizing step onset (summary plot in Figure 4C) and developed with kinetics well fit by single exponential functions (mean tau = 1.2 s; Figure 4D), consistent with previous work on ERG kinetics (Sturm et al., 2005, Wang et al., 1996, Wang et al., 1997a).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4D from 10 experiments.

claim: E-4031 reduced maximal light-sensitive outward current to ~20% of control magnitude.
source: Figure 4F summarizes the reduction in maximal light-sensitive outward current by E-4031 (to ~ 20% of control magnitude).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4F.

claim: E-4031 reduced tail current magnitude to 26% of control magnitude.
source: Figure 4G shows a similar reduction in tail current magnitude (to 26% of control magnitude) by E-4031.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4G.

claim: SK, M current, and ERG all contribute to spike frequency adaptation in L5 pyramidal cells.
source: While several previous studies described increased neuronal excitability following ChR2 stimulated ACh release (Joshi et al., 2016, Baker et al., 2018, Hedrick and Waters, 2015), we believe this is the first report that focuses on the continuous release of endogenous ACh throughout neocortical neuron discharges. Most of these previous studies found that optogenetic stimulation alone increased spontaneous firing (Baker et al., 2018 and NB electrical stimulation in Metherate et al., 1992) or promoting spontaneous firing in near-threshold neurons (Joshi et al., 2016, Hedrick and Waters, 2015) through activation of mAChRs.
evidence: This is an implicit claim based on the experimental results showing that blocking each of these currents affects SFA.

claim: Only SK modulators affected first spike latency; SK blocker NS8593 reduced firing latency while SK activator NS309 increased first spike latency.
source: We also determined whether any of the four K+ channel modulators or release of endogenous ACh affected the first AP latency in the same experiments. Only SK modulators affected first spike latency with the SK blocker NS8593 reducing the firing latency while the SK activator NS309 increasing the first spike latency (both p<0.05; Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Blockade of M current with XE991 failed to modulate first spike latency.
source: Blockade of M current with XE991 and ERG with Terf (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and E-4031 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A) all failed to modulate first spike latency (all p>0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 5E and supplementary figures.

claim: Blockade of ERG with Terf and E-4031 failed to modulate first spike latency.
source: Blockade of M current with XE991 and ERG with Terf (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and E-4031 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A) all failed to modulate first spike latency (all p>0.05).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 5E and supplementary figures.

claim: ChR2-stimulated release of endogenous ACh failed to modulate the first spike time.
source: ChR2-stimulated release of endogenous ACh also failed to modulate the first spike time (p>0.05; Figure 5F), providing additional evidence that endogenous ACh selectively modulated ERG without affecting SK-mediated currents.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SK currents are activated, at least in part, by sub-AP threshold Ca2+ influx, perhaps through T-type low-threshold VGCCs.
source: The bidirectional modulation of the first spike timing by NS8593 and NS309 implies that SK currents are activated, at least in part, by sub-AP threshold Ca2+ influx, perhaps through T-type low-threshold VGCCs. Previous studies (Wolfart and Roeper, 2002, Matschke et al., 2018) demonstrated close functional coupling between SK channels and T-type channels in other cell types, providing a potential mechanism to explain why SK channel modulators affected first spike latency in our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that SK modulators affect first spike latency, combined with citations to previous studies showing SK-T-type channel coupling.

claim: The rate of SFA reduction assessed by slope analysis was maximal during the first 200 ms of the step response with NS8593 and then decayed to a lower steady-state level at 500 ms.
source: As shown in left panel in Figure 6B, the rate of SFA reduction assessed using this method was maximal during the first time point assayed (200 ms into the step response) and then decayed until reaching a lower steady-state level at 500 ms into the step response.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B left panel.

claim: The effectiveness of adaptation mediated by M current was relatively constant throughout the step.
source: The effectiveness of adaptation mediated by M current, by contrast, was relatively constant throughout the step (middle panel in Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B middle panel.

claim: The rate of SFA increased during the step response when ERG currents were attenuated by Terf with high BAPTA internal.
source: As with the simulation example plot with linearly-increasing K+ current, the rate of SFA increased during the step both when ERG currents were attenuated by Terf with high BAPTA internal (right panel in Figure 6B) and when ChR2 stimulation released ACh (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B right panel.

claim: The rate of SFA increased during the step response when ChR2 stimulation released ACh.
source: As with the simulation example plot with linearly-increasing K+ current, the rate of SFA increased during the step both when ERG currents were attenuated by Terf with high BAPTA internal (right panel in Figure 6B) and when ChR2 stimulation released ACh (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claim: The adaptation mediated by SK NS8593-sensitive SK channels diminished during the step response.
source: In Figure 6D we compare the SFA rates at the beginning and end of the step response and find that the adaptation mediated by SK NS8593-sensitive SK channels diminished during the step response while, conversely, the adaptation mediated by ERG channels increased.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D.

claim: The adaptation mediated by ERG channels increased during the step response.
source: In Figure 6D we compare the SFA rates at the beginning and end of the step response and find that the adaptation mediated by SK NS8593-sensitive SK channels diminished during the step response while, conversely, the adaptation mediated by ERG channels increased.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6D.

claim: ChR2-stimulated ACh release modulated the SFA rate preferentially during the late phase of the step response.
source: Similar to Terf, ChR2-stimulated ACh release modulated the SFA rate preferentially during the late phase of the step response.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing early and late slope values in Figure 6D.

claim: Slightly depolarizing L5 pyramidal cells revealed persistent firing in response to coincident step + light stimuli.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, slightly depolarizing L5 pyramidal cells revealed persistent firing in response to coincident step + light stimuli.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 7A.

claim: No persistent firing occurred when the step depolarization was presented alone.
source: No persistent firing occurred when the step depolarization was presented alone (black trace in Figure 7A, right) or steps were paired with preceding or subsequent ChR2 stimulation (i.e., not coincident, c.f., Figure 1H; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 7A and supplementary figures.

claim: Persistent firing triggered by coincident ChR2 light/step stimulation required mAChR activation since it was abolished by atropine.
source: Persistent firing triggered by coincident ChR2 light/step stimulation required mAChR activation since it was abolished by atropine (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 7B.

claim: Muscarinic receptors activation with either endogenous ACh or CCh triggered persistent firing at similar frequencies (~5 Hz).
source: As shown in Figure 8A, muscarinic receptors activation with either endogenous ACh (orange) or CCh (green) triggered persistent firing at similar frequencies (~5 Hz; Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8A-B.

claim: 73% of L5 pyramidal cells in which ChR2 stimulation increased spike numbers had persistent firing lasting at least 2 s.
source: Among our population of L5 pyramidal cells in which ChR2 stimulation increased the number of spikes evoked during step stimuli, a majority (73%) had persistent firing that lasted at least 2 s following the depolarizing stimuli.
evidence: Reported as a summary statistic from the experimental population.

claim: 87% of L5 pyramidal cells tested with bath CCh had persistent firing.
source: In the same cell type, bath CCh also enabled persistent firing in large majority (87%) of cells tested (Figure 8C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8C.

claim: There was a large increase in input resistance during persistent firing which was maximal 2-3 s following step offset.
source: Using the same method based on trains of brief hyperpolarizing steps (Figure 8D, top) corrected by the effect of depolarization (using Rin vs membrane potential calibration data, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), we find a similar increase in input resistance during persistent firing which was maximal 2–3 s following step offset (Figure 8D, middle).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8D.

claim: The post-step increase in input resistance decayed with similar kinetics in both ChR2-ACh and bath CCh conditions.
source: The post-step increase in input resistance decayed with similar kinetics in both ChR2-ACh and bath CCh conditions (Figure 8D, bottom).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8D bottom panel.

claim: All three ERG antagonists tested (Terf, E-4031 and ErgToxin) abolished persistent firing in ChR2 experiments.
source: When we compared the ability of different K+ channel antagonists to block persistent firing gated by either endogenous ACh (via ChR2 stimulation) of bath CCh, we found similar results. All three structurally-diverse ERG antagonists tested (Terf, E-4031 and ErgToxin) abolished persistent firing in ChR2 (Figure 8E) and in our previously published (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) data set using bath CCh (Figure 8F).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8E.

claim: All three ERG antagonists tested abolished persistent firing in bath CCh experiments.
source: When we compared the ability of different K+ channel antagonists to block persistent firing gated by either endogenous ACh (via ChR2 stimulation) of bath CCh, we found similar results. All three structurally-diverse ERG antagonists tested (Terf, E-4031 and ErgToxin) abolished persistent firing in ChR2 (Figure 8E) and in our previously published (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) data set using bath CCh (Figure 8F).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8F from previously published data.

claim: Persistent firing following both ChR2 stimulation and bath CCh application was resistant to block by antagonists of the M current (XE991) and SK channels (NS8593).
source: Persistent firing following both ChR2 stimulation and bath CCh application was resistant to block by antagonists of the M current (XE991) and SK channels (NS8593).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: ChR2 stimulation increased SNR across virtual ensembles of L5 pyramidal cells.
source: Using similar methods to estimate SNR as employed in previous extracellular unit recordings in vivo (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009, McAdams and Maunsell, 1999), we find that ChR2 stimulation increased SNR across virtual ensembles of L5 pyramidal cells (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 9B-C.

claim: Reducing ERG-like linearly increasing K+ currents enhanced network SNR in computational models.
source: We also found that reducing ERG-like linearly increasing K+ currents enhanced network SNR in our computational models (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure 1.

claim: The increase in SNR with ChR2 stimulation was due to enhancements of signal while the noise component was not changed.
source: The increase in SNR in our experiments was due to enhancements of signal while the noise component was not changed (Figure 9D–E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 9D-E.

claim: ChR2-driven ACh release decreased pairwise signal correlations within virtual networks.
source: ChR2-driven ACh release also decreased pairwise signal correlations within virtual networks, an effect that we observed preferentially in response to stimuli lasting >650 ms.
evidence: Demonstrated through correlation analysis of virtual ensembles.

claim: Across 24 light-stimulated ACh release experiments, there was significantly less temporal signal correlation in responses acquired during light stimulation than in control conditions.
source: Across 24 light-stimulated ACh release experiments, we found significantly less temporal signal correlation in responses acquired during light stimulation than in control conditions.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical analysis of 24 experiments.

claim: ChR2 stimulation reduced the average signal correlation by 22% (from 0.27 to 0.21) considering all 276 pairwise comparisons.
source: Considering all 276 pairwise comparisons within our population of 24 experiments, ChR2 stimulation reduced the average signal correlation by 22% (from 0.27 to 0.21; Figure 10E).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 10E.

claim: ChR2 stimulation significantly reduced signal correlation (to p<0.01) only when responses longer than 625 ms were analyzed.
source: As shown in Figure 10F, ChR2 stimulation significantly reduced signal correlation (to p<0.01) only when responses longer than 625 ms were analyzed.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10F.

claim: The decrease in signal correlations in computer simulations where the ERG-like K+ current was attenuated was apparent with low to moderate discharge frequencies.
source: The decrease in signal correlations in computer simulations where the ERG-like K+ current was attenuated was apparent with low to moderate discharge frequencies, including the standardized ~ 10 Hz discharges examined in this study.
evidence: Demonstrated in computational simulations.

claim: Signal correlations between neurons with higher frequency discharges were modulated less by the linearly increasing K+ current, though they remained statistically different throughout the range of stimulus amplitudes tested.
source: Signal correlations between neurons with higher frequency discharges were modulated less by the linearly increasing K+ current, though they remained statistically different throughout the range of stimulus amplitudes tested in our model (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated in supplementary figure 1B.

claim: The coordinated reductions in ERG-like conductances across neurons within a cortical network are sufficient to reduce ensemble signal correlation.
source: These computational simulation results suggest that the coordinated reductions in ERG-like conductances across neurons within a cortical network are sufficient to reduce ensemble signal correlation and this effect was robust over a wide range of discharge frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: A component of network desynchronization may reflect attenuation of the 'baseline' temporal patterning imparted to most neuronal discharges by SFA.
source: The reduction in signal correlation also may underlie network desynchronization, since in our experiments, ACh appears to attenuate the slow temporal pattern imparted by each neuron's intrinsic physiology. These results suggest that a component of network desynchronization may reflect attenuation of the 'baseline' temporal patterning imparted to most neuronal discharges by SFA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Similar biophysiological modulation by ACh may be responsible for both LFP desynchronization and reduction in signal correlation.
source: Previous work has demonstrated the association between signal correlation and desynchronization in local field potential commonly observed in vivo upon NB stimulation (Metherate and Ashe, 1993, Kalmbach et al., 2012, Pinto et al., 2013). Dan and colleagues (Goard and Dan, 2009) assayed with both local field potential and unit recordings in rat visual cortex while presenting natural stimuli. Local field potential was desynchronized and signal correlation was also reduced upon NB electrical stimulation. These results suggest that similar biophysiological modulation by ACh may be responsible for both LFP desynchornization and reduction in signal correlation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between the authors' results and previous in vivo findings.

claim: Normal firing rate adaptation in L5 pyramidal cells likely reflects the effects of at least three different K+ currents recruited in a stereotyped order (first SK, then M, and then finally ERG).
source: We make three primary conclusions in this study. First, that the normal firing rate adaptation commonly observed in L5 pyramidal cells likely reflects the effects of at least three different K+ currents that are recruited in a stereotyped order (first SK, then M, and then finally ERG).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Coincident release of endogenous ACh during depolarizing stimuli selectively decreases the late phase of SFA by reducing ERG by activating muscarinic receptors.
source: Second, we find that coincident release of endogenous ACh during depolarizing stimuli selectively decreases the late phase of SFA by reducing ERG by activating muscarinic receptors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The preferential modulation of ERG by endogenous ACh enables cholinergic stimulation to selectively enhance responses to long-lasting stimuli while leaving responses to brief stimuli unaffected.
source: The preferential modulation of ERG by endogenous ACh enables cholinergic stimulation to selectively enhance responses to long-lasting stimuli while leaving responses to brief stimuli unaffected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing duration-dependent effects.

claim: The preferential modulation of a leak K+ current with slow kinetics explains the ability of cholinergic stimulation to enable persistent firing following depolarizing steps in quiescent neurons.
source: The preferential modulation of a leak K+ current with slow kinetics also explains the ability of cholinergic stimulation to enable persistent firing following depolarizing steps in quiescent neurons, a phenomenon widely reported following bath application of muscarinic receptor agonists (Egorov et al., 2002, Rahman and Berger, 2011, Knauer et al., 2013, Jochems and Yoshida, 2013, Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) but not reported previously following ChR2-stimulated release of endogenous ACh.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two phenomena associated with muscarinic cholinergic modulation (enhanced neuronal excitability and enabling persistent firing) are both mediated by attenuation of ERG currents.
source: Two phenomena associated with muscarinic cholinergic modulation of neuronal excitability (enhanced neuronal excitability and enabling persistent firing that outlasts the triggering depolarizing stimuli) are both mediated by attenuation of ERG currents.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The same ERG modulation mechanism that mediates the late phase of SFA can explain previously reported changes in signal-to-noise ratio and correlation properties assayed in network recordings in vivo.
source: And finally, we determined that the same ERG modulation mechanism that mediates the late phase of SFA can explain previously reported changes in the signal-to-noise ratio and correlation properties assayed in network recordings in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings and comparison with in vivo studies.

claim: Cholinergic inputs can modulate a specific subclass of K+ currents out of a larger constellation of potential candidate currents, leading to distinctive changes in intrinsic physiology.
source: Together, these findings reveal that cholinergic inputs can modulate a specific subclass of K+ currents out of a larger constellation of potential candidate currents, leading to distinctive changes in intrinsic physiology that can potentially explain many features of attention-related working memory tasks.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: SK-mediated AHP is assayed soon after a step-evoked burst of APs but is presumably active throughout spiking responses.
source: The Ca2+-dependent AHP response is assayed soon after a step-evoked burst of APs (Peron and Gabbiani, 2009, Ha and Cheong, 2017) but is presumably active throughout spiking responses, functioning to slow firing rates (Storm, 1989).
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies and general knowledge about SK channel function.

claim: Multiple studies implicated SK channels in mediating at least partially AHP and SFA.
source: Multiple studies implicated calcium-activated small-conductance K+ (SK) channels in mediating at least partially AHP and SFA (Bond et al., 2004, Pedarzani et al., 2005, Ji et al., 2009, Yen et al., 1999, Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Some adaptation remains following even strong Ca2+ chelation, indicating SK-mediated adaptation cannot be the sole mechanism.
source: While SK-mediated adaptation explains the common finding that increasing intracellular Ca2+ buffering reduces SFA, it cannot be the sole mechanism as some adaptation remains following even strong Ca2+ chelation (Madison and Nicoll, 1984, Storm, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have implicated K+ currents active near rest in contributing to SFA, including the M current and ERG.
source: Previous studies also have implicated K+ currents active near rest in contributing to SFA, including the M current (Aiken et al., 1995, Gu et al., 2005) and ERG (Chiesa et al., 1997, Sacco et al., 2003, Pessia et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Crill and colleagues identified three primary classes of AHPs based on kinetic differences, termed fast, medium and slow.
source: Crill and colleagues (Schwindt et al., 1988a, Spain et al., 1987, Schwindt et al., 1988, Schwindt et al., 1988b) identified three primary classes of AHPs based on kinetic differences, termed fast, medium and slow.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Crill and colleagues.

claim: BK channels contribute to the fastest AHP.
source: Based on more recent studies, big-conductance Ca2+ -activated K+ channels (BK) channels like contribute to the fastest AHP (Gu et al., 2005) while multiple currents appear contribute to the medium AHP, including SK channels (Schwindt et al., 1988a), I-H (Spain et al., 1987, Schwindt et al., 1988, Gu et al., 2005) and the M current (Storm, 1989, Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gu et al., 2005.

claim: Multiple currents contribute to the medium AHP, including SK channels, I-H, and the M current.
source: Based on more recent studies, big-conductance Ca2+ -activated K+ channels (BK) channels like contribute to the fastest AHP (Gu et al., 2005) while multiple currents appear contribute to the medium AHP, including SK channels (Schwindt et al., 1988a), I-H (Spain et al., 1987, Schwindt et al., 1988, Gu et al., 2005) and the M current (Storm, 1989, Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: ERG likely contributes to the slow AHP described in prior studies.
source: The identity of the K+ current mediating the slow AHP has remained elusive. Based on results in the present study, ERG likely contributes to the slow AHP described in these prior studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings in the present study.

claim: Previous work demonstrated the sensitivity of slow AHP to muscarinic receptor activation which evoked a coordinated reduction in slow AHP amplitude and SFA.
source: Previous work (Schwindt et al., 1988b) demonstrated the sensitivity of slow AHP to muscarinic receptor activation which evoked a coordinated reduction in slow AHP amplitude and SFA, paralleling results we obtained following ERG attenuation in the present study.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwindt et al., 1988b.

claim: SK current can be rapidly activated by subthreshold T-type Ca2+ current.
source: Previous work demonstrated that SK current can be rapidly activated by subthreshold T-type Ca2+ current (Wolfart and Roeper, 2002, Matschke et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: M currents have activation time constant of ~100 ms.
source: M currents are typically regarded as slow (although not as slow as ERG) K+ current with activation time constant of ~ 100 ms (Prole et al., 2003)–explaining the lack of first spike time modulation with XE991–while ERG is even slower with activation time constant of 1 ~ 2 s (Wang et al., 1997a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prole et al., 2003.

claim: ERG has activation time constant of 1-2 s.
source: M currents are typically regarded as slow (although not as slow as ERG) K+ current with activation time constant of ~ 100 ms (Prole et al., 2003)–explaining the lack of first spike time modulation with XE991–while ERG is even slower with activation time constant of 1 ~ 2 s (Wang et al., 1997a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 1997a.

claim: Several previous studies failed to find the initial first spike latency affected following M current blockade with linopirdine or XE991.
source: Consistent with our results, several previous studies also failed to find the initial first spike latency affected following M current blockade with either linopirdine (Aiken et al., 1995) or XE991 (Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All three K+ currents that contribute to SFA in L5 neocortical pyramidal cells (SK, M and ERG) have been reported to be attenuated following mAChR activation.
source: All three K+ currents we find contribute to SFA in L5 neocortical pyramidal cells (SK, M and ERG) have been reported to be attenuated following mAChR activation (Buchanan et al., 2010, Giessel and Sabatini, 2010, Suh and Hille, 2007, Hirdes et al., 2004, Shapiro et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Most previous studies of ChR2-stimulated ACh release found that optogenetic stimulation alone increased spontaneous firing or promoted spontaneous firing in near-threshold neurons through activation of mAChRs.
source: While several previous studies described increased neuronal excitability following ChR2 stimulated ACh release (Joshi et al., 2016, Baker et al., 2018, Hedrick and Waters, 2015), we believe this is the first report that focuses on the continuous release of endogenous ACh throughout neocortical neuron discharges. Most of these previous studies found that optogenetic stimulation alone increased spontaneous firing (Baker et al., 2018 and NB electrical stimulation in Metherate et al., 1992) or promoting spontaneous firing in near-threshold neurons (Joshi et al., 2016, Hedrick and Waters, 2015) through activation of mAChRs.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Baker et al. addressed coincident ACh and depolarizations by optogenetically stimulating cortical cholinergic fibers with a brief 5 ms pulse of light immediately preceding a 1500 ms depolarizing step and demonstrated increased excitability which was partially reduced by M current blockers.
source: Baker et al. (Baker et al., 2018) addressed coincident ACh and depolarizations by optogenetically stimulated cortical cholinergic fibers with a brief 5 ms pulse of light immediately preceding a 1500 ms depolarizing step and demonstrated increased excitability which was partially reduced by M current blockers. (This study did not test ERG blockers.)
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2018.

claim: Prefrontal cortex L5 pyramidal cells can be classified into PT or IT subtypes based on their projection targets.
source: In prefrontal cortex, L5 pyramidal cells can be classified into PT or IT subtypes based on their projection targets (Dembrow et al., 2010, Dembrow and Johnston, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The L5 pyramidal cells recorded in this study more closely resemble PT cells based on their sensitivity to mAChR activation, high sag ratio, similar input resistance, and similar AP threshold and width properties.
source: Based on previously reported intrinsic physiological properties of prefrontal cortical neurons, the L5 pyramidal cells we recorded from more closely resemble PT cells, reflecting their sensitivity to mAChR activation, high sag ratio and similar input resistance as well as similar AP threshold and width properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previously reported properties.

claim: Prefrontal PT cells do not show the marked SFA found in TeA L5 regular spiking neurons.
source: However, prefrontal PT do not show the marked SFA we find in TeA L5 regular spiking neurons.
evidence: This is a statement comparing the present findings with properties of prefrontal PT cells.

claim: Because of the slow activation and recovery kinetics of ERG, neocortical pyramidal cells remain hyperexcitable following many types of depolarizing stimuli when mAChRs are activated.
source: Because of the slow activation and recovery kinetics of ERG (Wang et al., 1997a, Hardman and Forsythe, 2009, Cui and Strowbridge, 2018), neocortical pyramidal cells remain hyperexcitable following many types of depolarizing stimuli when mAChRs are activated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known kinetics of ERG and experimental observations.

claim: Post-stimulus hyperexcitability reflects a transient reduction in the leak K+ current normally mediated by ERG, which can trigger persistent firing following step stimuli when neurons are maintained near their firing threshold.
source: Using bath application of muscarinic receptor agonists, we showed (Cui and Strowbridge, 2018) that this post-stimulus hyperexcitabilty reflects a transient reduction in the leak K+ current normally mediated by ERG, which can trigger persistent firing following step stimuli when neurons are maintained near their firing threshold.
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: This is the first report of ChR2-stimulated ACh release triggering persistent firing when paired with depolarizing step stimuli.
source: We believe this is the first report of ChR2-stimulated ACh release triggering persistent firing when paired with depolarizing step stimuli though this phenomenon has been widely reported following bath application of cholinergic agents in neocortical (Krnjević et al., 1971, Rahman and Berger, 2011), hippocampal (Jochems and Yoshida, 2013, Knauer et al., 2013) and entorhinal (Klink and Alonso, 1997, Egorov et al., 2002) neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding, supported by citations to previous studies using bath application.

claim: Baker et al. performed experiments pairing ChR2-driven ACh release with step stimuli and failed to find persistent firing.
source: While few studies assayed the effects of pairing ChR2-driven ACh release with step stimuli, Baker et al. (Baker et al., 2018) performed this experiment and failed to find persistent firing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2018.

claim: The difference in persistent firing results between this study and Baker et al. may reflect a requirement for ACh release throughout the discharge and potentially higher density of AAV-infected neurons with non-floxed ChR2 transcripts.
source: This difference with our results may reflect a requirement for ACh release throughout the discharge, as discussed above, as well as a potentially higher density of AAV-infected neurons with non-floxed ChR2 transcripts (versus injecting a floxed ChR2 virus in a ChAT-cre mouse, as employed in Baker et al., 2018 and Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for differences between studies.

claim: Wild type rodents used in this study do not have the enhanced spontaneous ACh release often associated with AAV-ChR2 infected ChAT-cre mouse lines.
source: In addition, the wild type rodents used in our study do not have the enhanced spontaneous ACh release often associated with AAV-ChR2 infected ChAT-cre mouse lines (Kolisnyk et al., 2013, Chen et al., 2018, Hedrick et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing enhanced spontaneous ACh release in ChAT-cre mice.

claim: Brief pulses of ACh may trigger different signaling cascades in mAChRs than prolonged application of non-physiological receptor agonists.
source: First, brief pulses of ACh may trigger different signaling cascades in mAChRs than prolonged application of non-physiological receptor agonists.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: The commonly used artificial cholinergic receptor agonist CCh preferentially binds to the high affinity orthosteric site while endogenous ACh preferentially binds to the lower affinity allosteric site.
source: Previous work has identified two distinct binding sites on mAChRs (Wamsley et al., 1997, Birdsall et al., 1978) and determined that the commonly used artificial cholinergic receptor agonist CCh preferentially binds to the high affinity orthosteric site (Larocca et al., 1987) while endogenous ACh preferentially binds to the lower affinity allosteric site (Kellar et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ligand binding at allosteric sites appears to bias the resulting signal cascades towards predominately Gq-based versus arrestin-based mechanisms.
source: Ligand binding at allosteric sites appears to bias the resulting signal cascades towards predominately Gq-based versus arrestin-based mechanisms.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about receptor signaling.

claim: Binding of CCh at the orthosteric site can efficiently recruit arrestin 3, which inhibits Gq-coupled signaling transduction.
source: Binding of CCh at the orthosteric site can efficiently recruit arrestin 3 (Davis et al., 2010), which inhibits Gq-coupled signaling transduction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Davis et al., 2010.

claim: Brief pulses of endogenous ACh may trigger ERG modulation via the G protein pathway while prolonged perfusion of artificial agonists like CCh may modulate additional currents by recruiting the arrestin pathway.
source: It is possible, therefore, that brief pulses of endogenous ACh trigger ERG modulation via the G protein pathway while prolonged perfusion of artificial agonists like CCh modulate additional currents by recruiting the arrestin pathway.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Roth and colleagues demonstrated a similar pattern of differential activation of signaling pathways originating at 5-HT2 receptors.
source: Recently, Roth and colleagues (Wacker et al., 2017) demonstrated a similar pattern of differential activation of signaling pathways originating at 5-HT2 receptors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wacker et al., 2017.

claim: ERG is expressed at high levels on dendrites while M (KCNQ) channels are predominantly expressed on the cell body and axons and SK channels on dendritic spines.
source: In addition, the potential targets of mAChR modulation we examined are likely located within different compartments. ERG is expressed at high levels on dendrites (Hardman and Forsythe, 2009, Westenbroek, 2009) while M (KCNQ) channels are predominantly expressed on the cell body and the axons of the neocortical neurons and SK channel on dendritic spines (Trimmer, 2015, Child and Benarroch, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spatial differences in channel localization may enable different subsets of cholinergic axons to selectively regulate different K+ currents.
source: These spatial differences may enable different subsets of cholinergic axons to selectively regulate different K+ currents.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Population SNR was enhanced by ACh because the SFA modulation preferentially increased the signal component while leaving the noise component unchanged.
source: By creating virtual ensembles from our ChR2 experiments, we showed that population SNR was enhanced by ACh because the SFA modulation preferentially increased the signal component while leaving the noise component unchanged.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of virtual ensembles.

claim: Both SNR and signal correlation effects appear to derive from a reduction in the ERG-mediated late phase of SFA as they were reproduced in computational models that varied the density of an ERG-like linearly increasing K+ current.
source: Both SNR and signal correlation effects appear to derive from a reduction in the ERG-mediated late phase of SFA as they were reproduced in computational models that varied the density of an ERG-like linearly increasing K+ current.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling.

claim: Neither SNR nor signal correlation effect reflects a trivial result expected from any modulation that enhances excitability.
source: Neither SNR nor signal correlation effect reflects a trivial result expected from any modulation that enhances excitability. Indeed, reducing a temporally uniform K+ current would not be expected to change network signal correlation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specific nature of the modulation.

claim: Both SNR and signal correlation effects recapitulate commonly reported network signatures of cholinergic stimulation and attention in vivo.
source: Both SNR and signal correlation effect recapitulate commonly reported network signatures of cholinergic stimulation (Metherate et al., 1992, Kalmbach et al., 2012, Pinto et al., 2013, Goard and Dan, 2009, Minces et al., 2017) and attention (Pfurtscheller et al., 1999, Fries et al., 2001) in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous in vivo studies.

claim: Changes in intrinsic properties such as SFA could contribute to the statistical properties that distinguish different network states associated with behavioral conditions.
source: The similarity between these in vivo results and our experimental results raises the possibility that changes in intrinsic properties such as SFA could contribute to the statistical properties that distinguish different network states associated with behavioral conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between experimental and in vivo results.

claim: Computational results indicate that simply reducing SFA is sufficient to decrease network signal correlation.
source: Computational results, however, indicate that simply reducing SFA is sufficient to decrease network signal correlation (Wang et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014b.

claim: Strong SFA promotes similar discharge kinetics within networks and likely functions to enhance decoding ability.
source: Strong SFA promotes similar discharge kinetics within networks and likely functions to enhanced decoding ability (Cortes et al., 2012, Farkhooi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreasing SFA reduces the temporal patterning of discharges, likely increasing heterogeneity among constituent neurons and enabling greater information content within networks.
source: Conversely, decreasing SFA reduces the temporal patterning of discharges, likely increasing heterogeneity among constituent neurons and enabling greater information content within networks (Goard and Dan, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goard and Dan, 2009.

claim: Different modulatory systems likely influence discharge patterning by selectively reducing individual currents involved in different phases of SFA.
source: Our results indicate that different modulatory systems likely influence discharge patterning by selectively reducing individual currents involved in different phases of SFA, allowing for both simple gain control operations (e.g., by attenuating the quasi-static M current) and more complex manipulations that affect network SNR and correlation statistics when strongly time-dependent currents like ERG are modulated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Selectively altering the late-developing ERG current restricts the modulation to subsets of neurons with discharges long enough to be slowed by ERG while leaving brief responses unaffected.
source: In addition, selectively altering the late-developing ERG current has the additional effect of restricting the modulation to subsets of neurons–those with discharges long enough to be slowed by ERG–while leaving brief responses unaffected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing duration-dependent effects.

claim: The selective modulation of ERG by endogenous ACh may help explain the mechanisms of actions of schizophrenia treatments, many of which target cholinergic systems and also modulate ERG.
source: The selective modulation of ERG by endogenous ACh also may help explain the mechanisms of actions of schizophrenia treatments, many of which target cholinergic systems (Freedman, 2014, Cohen, 1944) and also modulate ERG (Wible et al., 2005, Cockerill et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The efficacy of cholinergic agents in schizophrenia have led many researchers to propose that dysfunction of ACh modulation underlies many aspects of this disease.
source: The efficacy of cholinergic agents in schizophrenia have lead many researchers to propose that dysfunction of ACh modulation underlies many aspects of this disease (Higley and Picciotto, 2014, Sarter and Bruno, 1998, Tandon et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous genetic work implicated ERG mutations in a subset of schizophrenic patients.
source: Previous genetic work implicated ERG mutations in a subset of schizophrenic patients (Apud et al., 2012, Hashimoto et al., 2013, Atalar et al., 2010, Huffaker et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: The most frequent schizophrenia-associated ERG mutation is located on a non-coding (intron) site and promotes transcription from an alternative transcription start site.
source: While the location of most frequent schizophrenia-associated ERG mutation is located on a non-coding (intron) site, previous work (Huffaker et al., 2009) demonstrated that this mutation promoted transcription from an alternative transcription start site.
evidence: Supported by citation to Huffaker et al., 2009.

claim: The isoforms resulting from the schizophrenia-associated ERG intron mutation were modified (affecting the ERG1 subunit), leading to altered gating properties and reduced ERG currents in heterologous expression systems.
source: The isoforms resulting from this intron mutation were modified (affecting the ERG1 subunit), leading to altered gating properties and reduced ERG currents when assayed in heterologous expression systems (Huffaker et al., 2009, Heide et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huffaker et al., 2009 and Heide et al., 2012.

claim: Some aspects of schizophrenia, especially positive symptoms such as psychosis, may relate to altered cortical excitability produced by abnormal ERG currents.
source: Our present results raise the possibility that some aspects of schizophrenia, especially positive symptoms such as psychosis, may relate to altered cortical excitability produced by abnormal ERG currents and suggest novel therapeutic approaches based on ERG-modulating agents (Wible et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and previous literature.
